paper_title: Improving Atomic-Fact Recall via Focused Views in Unstructured Knowledge Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as general-purpose interfaces to factual knowledge, but their parameters do not automatically reflect information that changes after pretraining. Knowledge editing (KE) provides a targeted alternative to costly retraining by modifying selected knowledge and preserving unrelated knowledge and general capabilities. Conventional KE uses structured factual triples, whereas unstructured KE (UKE) uses free-form passages containing multiple facts. Nonetheless, existing UKE editors exhibit a failure mode known as context reliance: edited LLMs can often reproduce the editing passage but fail to reliably recall its individual facts without the original passage context. We identify context-induced difficulty underestimation under the standard passage-level editing objective: later facts receive increasingly rich ground-truth context and consequently incur lower initial losses, making them appear easier to learn. In response, we propose FOVEATED, a plug-and-play framework that constructs focused views of each sentence by randomly shifting the Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) positions assigned to the keys of its preceding context. The perturbation is applied during editing and removed afterward, leaving the model's native positional encoding unchanged at inference time. We instantiate FOVEATED for both direct-optimization and locate-then-edit editors. We theoretically analyze how FOVEATED counteracts context-induced difficulty underestimation and empirically demonstrate consistent improvements across five KE editors, two LLM backbones, and three benchmarks.

Keywords: Knowledge Editing, Large Language Models Date: 2026-10-05 Contact: tliu43@tennessee.edu 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have become foundation for modern natural language processing tasks (Vaswani et al., 2017, Brown et al., 2020, Zhou et al., 2023). As model scale continues to grow, these capabilities make LLMs increasingly useful as general-purpose interfaces for accessing and reasoning with knowledge (Bommasani et al., 2021, Roberts et al., 2020, Kojima et al., 2022). However, an LLMs parametric knowledge remains largely fixed after pretraining and can quickly become outdated as real-world knowledge evolves, leading to factual errors in downstream applications (De Cao et al., 2021, Hartvigsen et al., 2023). Keeping the model current through repeated retraining is prohibitively expensive. As remedy, knowledge editing (KE) addresses this problem by incorporating specific new knowledge through selective model updates and preserving unrelated knowledge and general capabilities (Wang et al., 2023, Yao et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2024b). Standard KE typically represents new knowledge as separate factual association, often (subject, relation, These authors contributed equally to this work. Improving Atomic-Fact Recall via Focused Views in Unstructured Knowledge Editing object) triple. Given such structured facts, some methods directly optimize selected parameters (Wang et al., 2024a,b), while locate-then-edit (LTE) methods first identify where the target knowledge is represented and then write targeted update into the corresponding layers (Meng et al., 2022, 2023, Fang et al., 2025). Recent work relaxes this structured-input assumption through unstructured knowledge editing (UKE), where the new knowledge is provided as free-form passage (Wu et al., 2024a, Yang et al., 2025). Unlike structured edit, such passage may express multiple interrelated facts without specifying which ones user may later query. UKE methods accordingly expand the editable modules and decompose the passage into smaller units and coordinate their updates (Deng et al., 2025, Jiang et al., 2025, Su et al., 2025). Together, these methods expand the scope of KE from individual factual associations to free-form passages. Nonetheless, existing methods often fall short of making effective use of the edited knowledge beyond the original editing context. In particular, an edited model may recall the complete passage under the original editing query, yet fail to retrieve the new knowledge when answering more targeted questions about individual facts (Zhou et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026). Recent studies have begun to examine this failure mode, termed context reliance, in which the new knowledge may remain accessible only as part of the complete passage, where the edited model can rely on the preceding context as shortcut during generation. To mitigate this problem, Zhou et al. (2026) align predictions under global and local contexts; Wang et al. (2026) synthesize atomic questionanswer supervision with external models; and Liu et al. (2026) construct hybrid self-distillation trajectories from privileged in-context state. Yet the learning dynamics underlying context reliance remain underexplored. In light of this gap, we examine how context affects the apparent learning difficulty under the standard passage-level objective in this work. Interestingly, we find that the pre-update editing loss decreases for facts appearing later in the passage, even though all edited facts are new to the model (Wu et al., 2024a, Deng et al., 2025). Intuitively, under teacher forcing (Lamb et al., 2016), later content is predicted from longer ground-truth prefixes and thus receives richer contextual support. This growing support acts as shortcut, lowering the initial losses of later facts and making them appear easier to learn. We call this context-induced difficulty underestimation; Sec. 2 details our analysis. This observation is the first contribution of this work. In response, we propose FOVEATED to construct focused views that make the preceding context less reliable as shortcut during editing. By varying how target sentence retrieves its preceding context while preserving the sentence itself, FOVEATED trains the model on each fact across randomized contextual views and directs the editing signal toward the target content. Concretely, FOVEATED constructs such views by randomly shifting the key-side Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE; Su et al., 2021) positions assigned to the prompt and preceding sentences, while leaving all query rotations and the target sentences key rotations unchanged. The perturbation is applied only during editing and removed afterward, leaving the models native positional encoding unchanged at inference time. We further provide theoretical support for the focused-view design. FOVEATED is flexible framework that intervenes in the editing computation without prescribing how the updates are parameterized. It can be applied to wide range of existing editors, and we instantiate FOVEATED for two broad families. Direct optimization (DO) editors update selected parameters with gradient descent (Hu et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2024a,b, Liu et al., 2025b). For this family, FOVEATED generalizes the standard passage-level objective to weighted expectation of sentence-level losses under focused views. Setting the perturbation magnitude to zero exactly recovers the standard passage-level objective. For LTE editors (Deng et al., 2025, Su et al., 2025), applying FOVEATED is less direct because their passage objectives optimize intermediate hidden targets rather than the eventual parameter updates. We follow Wang et al. (2026) and adopt two-stage design by first writing sentence-level targets into shallow layers and then applying the base editor in deeper layers to learn the complete passage. The key distinction of our approach is that FOVEATED obtains its sentence-level targets directly from the editing passage under Improving Atomic-Fact Recall via Focused Views in Unstructured Knowledge Editing Figure 1: Pre-edit NLL loss in UnFine passages. Native loss gradually decreases toward later passage positions, and FOVEATED views yield consistently higher losses at the same positions. focused views, without synthesizing atomic questionanswer supervision through external models. See Sec. 3 for details. This general editing framework and our theoretical analysis form the main technical contribution of this work. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. 2 introduces context-induced difficulty underestimation, Sec. 3 presents FOVEATED and its theoretical analysis, and Sec. 4 evaluates the method. Secs. 5 and 6 review related work and conclude the paper, respectively. 2. When that context is absent, the edited LLMs struggle to recall the new knowledge, especially facts appearing later in the passage. Such failure limits the effectiveness of UKE beyond the original editing context. Whereas this pattern appears to be contextual overfitting problem of KE (Zhang et al., 2024a, Liu et al., 2025a), we show that it is analogous to underfitting: the presence of contextual support makes new knowledge appear easy to predict even when the LLM has not sufficiently learned it. Specifically, although (U)KE methods differ in the variables they optimize to incorporate new knowledge (Fang et al., 2025, Jiang et al., 2025), their supervision often comes from fitting the editing passage through negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss (Liu et al., 2025a). Intuitively, the prefix provides increasingly rich context as the passage unfolds. Consequently, even if the LLM does not yet hold the new knowledge, it can still see the fact as plausible continuation of the surrounding text. This contextual shortcut can make the loss understate the difficulty of acquiring the knowledge. We call this effect context-induced difficulty underestimation. To examine the effect empirically, we evaluate Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) on free-form passages from UnFine (Wang et al., 2026) and measure the initial token-level NLL before any editing updates. Although these passages are designed to contain new knowledge throughout (Deng et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2026), Fig. 1 shows clear decrease in initial loss toward later positions. Later content thus appears easier to predict despite still introducing new knowledge, consistent with the growing prefix providing contextual support before the model has learned anything from the edit. To test whether intrinsic sentence difficulty explains the decline, we randomly shuffle the sentence order in each passage and observe the same pattern (App. D.1). Experiments We evaluate FOVEATED with five UKE editors spanning the DO and LTE families. 4.1. Experimental Setup Base Models. We select two LLMs widely used in UKE studies (Jiang et al., 2025, Su et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026): Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Dubey et al., 2024), which we refer to as Qwen2.5 and Llama3.1, respectively. Tasks. We use UnFine (Wang et al., 2026), which augments existing benchmarks to enable finer-grained evaluation of UKE. It contains three subsets: (1) UnFine-UnKE extends UnKEBench (Deng et al., 2025); (2) UnFine-CF and (3) UnFine-MQ extend the CounterFact (Meng et al., 2022) and MQuAKE (Zhong et al., 2023) subsets of Wu et al. (2024a), respectively. We adopt the single-request setting from prior UKE work (Deng et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2026). Editing Methods. We evaluate FOVEATED on five editing methods spanning both DO and LTE families. Among the DO editors, FT-M (Zhang et al., 2024b) fine-tunes the MLP layer identified by causal tracing, LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) learns additive low-rank updates to model parameters, and simplified variant of (Zhou et al., 2026) fine-tunes the model on the passage and regularizes against context reliance2. Implementation details are provided in App. C. We report computation overhead of FOVEATED in App. D.5. FOVEATED adds moderate editing overhead but no inference cost. Evaluation. Related Work Knowledge Editing aims to update specific factual knowledge in pretrained model and preserve unrelated knowledge and the models general capabilities (Wang et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2024b). Optimization-based approaches learn model updates with the editing objective, including selected layer optimization (Zhang et al., 2024b) or learning multiple copies (Wang et al., 2024b). Parameter-efficient methods have also been applied (Hu et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2024a, Wu et al., 2024b, Liu et al., 2025b). On the other hand, Locate-Then-Edit (LTE) methods first identify where fact is stored, then compute the weight change often in closed form (Meng et al., 2022, 2023, Li et al., 2024, Fang et al., 2025). Unstructured Knowledge Editing (UKE) replaces the curated triple with free-form passage (Wu et al., 2024a, Yang et al., 2025). UnKE makes transformer blocks editable (Deng et al., 2025), AnyEdit decomposes passages into sequential chunks (Jiang et al., 2025), and µKE coordinates sentence-level updates through nested editing structure (Su et al., 2025). COIN identifies context reliance during editing and mitigates it by aligning predictions under global and local contexts (Zhou et al., 2026). FABLE uses externally synthesized atomic-QA supervision to write shallow-layer anchors before fitting the passage holistically, and introduces UnFine to measure atomic-fact access (Wang et al., 2026). In concurrent work, HPSE uses hybrid rollouts to recover missing facts with token-level feedback from privileged in-context state (Liu et al., 2026). In contrast, our FOVEATED targets the learning signal by disrupting contextual support that can suppress gradients before fact becomes independently retrievable. Positional Encoding. RoPE encodes relative positions by rotating queries and keys (Su et al., 2021) and is widely used in modern LLMs (Dubey et al., 2024, Qwen Team, 2024, Liu et al., 2024). Long-context adaptation also manipulates positions: Peng et al. (2024) scale RoPE frequencies and attention, Zhu et al. (2024) shift the indices of entire chunks, and Li et al. (2026) shift suffix indices and distill the perturbed view from native-view predictions. These methods perturb positions to improve the models tolerance to positional variation. FOVEATED instead uses perturbation for fundamentally different purpose: by randomizing only preceding-context keys and supervising with ground truth rather than native-view predictions, it breaks contextual shortcuts and makes the edited fact robust across contexts. 6. Conclusion In this work, we identify context-induced difficulty underestimation in UKE and propose FOVEATED, which constructs focused positional views to make contextual shortcuts less reliable during editing. Across five editors, two LLM backbones, and three benchmarks, FOVEATED broadly improves fine-grained fact recall and retains holistic recall. Encouraged by these consistent improvements, we plan to extend FOVEATED to handle correlated, continually evolving unstructured knowledge, where new updates may reinforce, revise, or invalidate earlier ones. By tracking these dependencies and selectively preserving or revising previously edited knowledge, we aim to pave the way toward practical UKE in continuously changing real-world environments.

All evaluations query the edited model without supplying the editing passage. We use greedy decoding and cap D3 generations at 30 new tokens, with the instruction Answer directly and keep your 37 Improving Atomic-Fact Recall via Focused Views in Unstructured Knowledge Editing answer within 20 words. The original and paraphrased queries (Orig Q/Reph Q) carry no additional instruction. Holistic recall. We compute ROUGE-L recall against the complete editing passage. For each request, we report the original query (Orig Q), its paraphrase (Reph Q), and their average as an overall measure. the generated Atomic-fact recall. For request with atomic questions, let aj answer, and 𝒫j the annotated key phrases for question j. We average ROUGE-L recall over the questions. Following the UnFine implementation (Wang et al., 2026), HR counts key phrase as recovered only when all its words appear in order in the generation, and LCS computes the word-level longest common subsequence length: be the reference answer, ˆaj j= HR = p𝒫j I[LCS(p, ˆaj) = p] j=1 𝒫j , CLCS = 1 j=1 LCS(aj, ˆaj) aj . We follow Wang et al. (2026) for the computation of the metrics. Namely, ROUGE-L is computed with the rouge packages default preprocessing. For HR and CLCS , we lowercase the text and extract alphanumeric words using [A-Za-z0-9]+; generated answers are also stripped of chat end markers and trailing periods. C.3. General Capability Evaluation Datasets Following Wang et al. (2026), Zhou et al. (2026), we evaluate post-editing general capabilities on six benchmarks: SST-2 (Socher et al., 2013) (sentiment), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) (knowledge and reasoning), MRPC (Dolan and Brockett, 2005) (paraphrase detection), CoLA (Warstadt et al., 2019) (grammatical acceptability), RTE (Bentivogli et al., 2009) (textual entailment), and NLI (Williams et al., 2018) (natural language inference). We report likelihood-based F1 scores using the codebase of Wang et al. (2026). D. Additional Results This section presents results omitted from the main text. D.1. Sentence-Order Effect for Pre-Edit Loss In this section, we study the effect of sentence order on pre-edit loss to test whether the positional decline is caused by intrinsic sentence difficulty. We randomly shuffle the sentences within each UnFine passage and recompute their pre-edit losses using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Since shuffling can make the original editing query inconsistent with the reordered passage, we use the order-insensitive prompt Introduce for both the original and shuffled conditions, where is the edited subject. Results are shown in Fig. 4. Across all three datasets, pre-edit loss still decreases with passage position after shuffling. This rules out sentence order as the cause and further supports context-induced difficulty underestimation. Improving Atomic-Fact Recall via Focused Views in Unstructured Knowledge Editing Figure 4: Pre-edit loss by passage position under the original and randomly shuffled sentence orders. Both conditions use the order-insensitive prompt Introduce X. The positional decline persists after shuffling. D.2. Scores are reported to one decimal place. D.3. General Capability Scores Tab. 12 reports general-capability scores after editing. See App. C.3 for evaluation details. D.4. Sensitivity Analysis on Perturbation Scale Tab. 13 reports the sensitivity of FOVEATED to perturbation scale σ when applied to FT-M and µKE. From the table, we see that the effective range of σ depends on the specific editor. For FT-M, moderate perturbation improves atomic-fact recall and retains holistic performance, whereas larger scales substantially degrade holistic recall. In contrast, µKE benefits from nonzero perturbation and remains broadly stable for σ [4, 32]. Accordingly, we use σ = 1 for FT-M and σ = 16 for µKE. D.5. Editing Cost FOVEATED trades additional editing time for improved atomic-fact recall. The FT-M editor call increases from 3.06 to 13.72 seconds per edit with nearly unchanged peak memory; for µKE, it increases from 5.69 to 21.34 seconds, with peak memory rising from 18.33 to 23.17 GB. Profiling attributes the LTE increase to its first-stage sentence residual optimization (approximately 10.5 seconds) and shallow closed-form write (approximately 5.1 seconds), while the base µKE stage remains 5.66.2 seconds. Focused views are disabled after editing, so generation and evaluation incur no method-specific runtime or memory overhead. D.6.
